analysis.one_liner: Charges mining companies a royalty for minerals taken from federal land, with proceeds cleaning up abandoned mines.
analysis.headline: A bill requiring hardrock miners to pay the federal government a 5% royalty died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 1872 General Mining Law, companies can dig gold, silver, copper and other minerals from federal public land and pay nothing to the treasury, and can even buy the land outright for old-law prices. This bill would charge a 5% royalty on the value of minerals extracted, put the money into a fund to clean up abandoned hardrock mines, stop new patents (land sales) except for old applications, and charge annual fees of $100-$125 per claim. It was referred to the House Resources Committee and its subcommittee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who currently receive nothing for minerals taken from public land, and residents of western communities living with the pollution, poisoned water, and dangerous open shafts left by abandoned mines, since royalty money would fund reclamation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines

how_it_helps.text: Requires a 5% royalty on the net smelter return of locatable minerals produced from claims under the general mining laws, so the federal government collects revenue from mineral extraction on public land for the first time under those laws.

Deposits all royalty and claim-fee receipts into an Abandoned Minerals Mine Reclamation Fund to reclaim abandoned surface and deep mines, seal mine entries, and prevent, treat, and control water pollution from abandoned mine drainage.

Bars the government from issuing new patents — outright title to mining and mill site claims — unless the application was filed and requirements met by September 30, 1994, ending new transfers of public land to private owners under 19th-century terms.
Imposes annual claim maintenance fees of $100 per claim held before enactment and $125 for new claims, with a waiver for holders of 10 or fewer claims, so small claimants are spared the cost.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies — producers of gold, silver, copper, and other locatable minerals on federal land — who would pay the royalty, the annual fees, and face auditing and civil penalties for false reporting.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on public land

drawbacks.text: A 5% royalty is modest, but any royalty raises costs at the margin and could make some low-grade mines uneconomic, costing jobs in rural western mining towns.
Operators face quarterly reporting, technical and financial disclosure to the Interior Secretary, audits, and civil penalties up to $10,000 for false or missing reports.
Reclamation spending depends on the fund being appropriated, so cleanup of abandoned mines is not guaranteed even if royalties flow in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but limited: a 5% royalty is on the low end of what mineral royalties run, and reclamation spending depends on annual appropriations. The main costs fall on a specific industry that today pays nothing for public minerals, though some marginal mines and jobs could be lost. The bill was a moderate reform, not a sweeping one, and its modesty is partly explained by the political difficulty of touching the mining industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Resources Committee, then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it sat; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller of California, joined by Rep. Nick Rahall, introduced the bill on February 13, 1997, to secure a federal return on minerals extracted from public domain lands.
The House referred it to the Committee on Resources the same day.
On February 21, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources and the Interior Department was asked for its comments — the last action ever taken on the bill.
The bill had 23 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never advanced out of committee in the Republican-controlled 105th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies, which continued to extract minerals from federal land royalty-free and could pursue patents under the old rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

sides.party_line_note: All 24 members backing the bill — the sponsor and 23 cosponsors — were Democrats; the Republican-controlled Resources Committee, which held the bill, took no action on it.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, silver, copper and other locatable minerals)
industries.note: The bill would end a century-old arrangement in which companies pay no royalty for minerals taken from federal land, charge them annual claim fees, and cut off new land patents. What the companies would pay is money the public currently forgoes, and some of it would fund cleanup of mine waste the industry's operations left behind.
